For Robert Philen You are like me, you will die too, but not today: you, incommensurate, therefore the hours shine: if I say to you “To you I say,” you have not been set to music, or broadcast live on the ghost radio, may never be an oil painting or Old Master’s charcoal sketch: you are a concordance of person, number, voice, and place, strawberries spread through your name as if it were budding shrubs, how you remind me of some spring, the waters as cool and clear (late rain clings to your leaves, shaken by light wind), which is where you occur in grassy moonlight: and you are a lily, an aster, white trillium or viburnum, by all rights mine, white star in the meadow sky, the snow still arriving from its earthwards journeys, here where there is no snow (I dreamed the snow was you, when there was snow), you are my right, have come to be my night (your body takes on the dimensions of sleep, the shape of sleep becomes you): and you fall from the sky with several flowers, words spill from your mouth in waves, your lips taste like the sea, salt-sweet (trees and seas have flown away, I call it loving you): home is nowhere, therefore you, a kind of dwell and welcome, song after all, and free of any eden we can name

For Robert Philen

You are like me—you, too, will die, but not today: you, incommensurable, and so the hours shine: if I say to you, "To you I say," still you have not been set to music, nor broadcast live on the ghost radio, may never become an oil painting or an Old Master's charcoal sketch: you are a concordance of person, number, voice, and place, strawberries threading through your name as though it were a budding shrub, how you call to mind some spring, its waters cool and clear (late rain still clings to your leaves, trembling in a light wind)—this is where you occur, in grassy moonlight: and you are a lily, an aster, a white trillium or viburnum, mine by every right, a white star fixed in the meadow sky, the snow still falling on its long descent to earth, here where no snow falls (I dreamed the snow was you, back when there was snow)—you are my right, you have become my night (your body assumes the dimensions of sleep, the shape of sleep becomes you): and you fall from the sky trailing flowers, words spill from your mouth in waves, your lips taste of the sea, salt-sweet (trees and seas have taken flight, and this is what I call loving you): home is nowhere, and so you are a kind of dwelling, a welcome, a song after all—free of any Eden we could ever name.

For Robert Philen

Like myself, you carry mortality within you, though death is not yet your appointment: your immeasurable nature makes the hours gleam brighter still. When I address you directly—"it is you I speak to"—no melody has claimed your name, no ghostly airwaves have carried your voice, no canvas or Old Master's charcoal has captured your likeness: you exist instead as harmony itself—of self, of number, of voice, of place. Your name blooms with strawberries as though it were a flowering thicket, calling to mind some hidden spring where waters run clear and cold (rain from yesterday still clings to your foliage, trembling in a gentle breeze), and this is where I find you, moving through moonlit grass: you are lily and aster both, white trillium, viburnum—rightfully mine, a pale star fixed in the meadow's sky, while snow continues its descent toward earth even here, in this place untouched by snow (I once dreamed the falling snow was you, back when snow still fell). You belong to me by right, you have become my darkness (your form takes on sleep's very shape, sleep's contours becoming your own): you descend from above scattered with blossoms, your speech pours forth in rolling waves, and your mouth carries the ocean's flavor, both salt and sweet (the forests and the seas have vanished into flight—this, I understand, is what it means to love you): there exists no true home, and so you become my shelter and my greeting, ultimately a song, unbound by any paradise we might try to name.
outputs.L3:
# On the Incomparable Beloved

There is a peculiar honesty in acknowledging that we, too, are mortal—that the same hourglass empties for both speaker and beloved, grain by grain, without mercy or exception. And yet within this shared frailty, something extraordinary asserts itself: the insistence that this particular person, despite belonging to the same doomed category as all others, remains utterly without equal. No substitution could ever suffice. No other presence could occupy the space this one fills. It is this paradox—mortality shared, uniqueness absolute—that makes time itself glow, as though each ordinary hour were suddenly lit from within simply because this person exists to inhabit it.

The beloved, however, refuses to be captured. Not by melody, not by the reach of broadcast or fame, not even by the patient hand of the portraitist. Every attempt to fix this person into art or image seems to slide off, insufficient, beside the point. And yet this resistance to representation is not emptiness—it is fullness of another order. The beloved possesses a wholeness that feels almost grammatical, as if they were the very syntax by which meaning becomes possible, the structure beneath language rather than a subject language could adequately describe. To know them is to sense completeness that has no need of external validation, fame, or artistic translation.

This wholeness expresses itself most vividly through nature's own vocabulary. Strawberries, springs, lilies, asters, snow—these are not mere metaphors but almost interchangeable identities, as though the beloved were seasons themselves, cycling through the sweetness of summer fruit, the sudden emergence of flowers, the hush of winter's first snowfall. The line between person and landscape dissolves entirely; to speak of the beloved is, inevitably, to speak of orchards and blooming fields and frost-covered ground, each image bleeding into the next until identity and terrain become indistinguishable.

There is possessiveness here too—an unapologetic claim, "my right," as though the beloved were not simply loved but *owned* in some fundamental, unrefusable sense. And yet this claiming is not domination; it is closer to belonging. The beloved becomes the very source of rest, the origin of night itself. Sleep does not simply occur in their presence—sleep *takes their form*, becomes shaped like them, so that even unconsciousness carries the imprint of their being.

And so the poem arrives, finally, at its quiet revelation: home is not a place. It is not some mythic garden, no matter how idealized, no matter how often imagined as paradise regained. True belonging is not geography, not Eden, not any fixed location on a map of longing. It is the beloved's presence—their welcome, their song—that constitutes home. Wherever they are is shelter enough. Whatever they offer is Eden enough. The search for paradise ends not in a place remembered or promised, but in a person, singular and irreplaceable, who transforms mere time into something luminous, and mere rest into something sacred.

# Untitled Poem (Expanded from Summary)

## I.

Let me tell you what I have seen in you—
not metaphor, exactly, but the closest
language comes to naming what refuses naming.

You are like the flower that opens once
and means it, means the whole brief blaze
of unrepeatable color, the petal
that will not fold back into bud
no matter how the season begs.

You are like water that has never
been this water before—not the river
downstream, not the rain an hour from now,
but this, moving past this rock, this light,
this exact configuration of current
that will not come again.

## II.

Consider the snow: how it falls
as if the sky were finally saying
something it could not say in words,
each flake a small unrepeatable theorem,
each one dissolving the moment it proves
its own singular architecture.

I have watched winter give way to spring
the way grief sometimes gives way to memory—
not forgetting, but transformation,
the seasons turning like a wheel
that somehow never touches
the same ground twice.

This is what I mean when I say *you*:
not a fixed point but a weather system,
not a single flower but the whole
astonishing fact of blooming.

## III.

They will tell you love can be captured.
They will offer you the recording,
the photograph, the perfect
reproduction—

Here, they will say, is the sound of her laughing.
Here is her face painted true to life.
Here is the poem that finally gets it right.

But I have listened to the recordings.
I have stood before the paintings.
I have read the poems that claim
to hold what cannot be held,
and always—always—there is the same
hollow at the center,
the same essential absence
where presence should be.

The music is not the moment.
The photograph is not the face
turning toward you in actual light,
in the specific gravity
of an actual room.

Even the broadcast, that miracle
of distance collapsed, that voice
traveling through wires and air
to reach you instantly—

it is not your voice.
It is not you, arriving.

## IV.

They will tell you about paradise, too—
some garden before gardens, some perfect
symmetry of trees and rivers,
some myth where nothing dies
and nothing changes and therefore
nothing means what mortal things mean.

I have heard the stories.
I understand their comfort,
the way they promise an ending
to all this aching impermanence.

But I do not want that garden.
I do not want the flower
that never wilts, the river
that never reaches the sea,
the winter that never surrenders
to spring's insistent green.

I want this:
the actual flower, dying as it blooms.
The actual river, becoming something else
with every mile.
The actual snow, brief
as a held breath, brief
as the space between
one word and the next.

## V.

So let me try again to say it:
home is not a paradise remembered
or a paradise promised.
Home is not the recording,
not the photograph, not the poem
that claims to have captured you.

Home is this—
your actual hand in actual light,
your actual voice saying my name
in a way no broadcast could replicate,
no matter how many miles
it managed to erase.

Home is the flower that will not last.
Home is the water that will not return.
Home is the snow that means everything
precisely because it cannot stay,
the season that must turn
because turning is the only way
it knows to keep its promise.

You are not the myth of paradise.
You are not the art that tries to hold you.

You are the mortal, particular fact
of yourself—
irreplaceable,
impossible to reproduce,
here.

This is what I have been trying to say:
you are not like anything.
You are the thing itself.
And I have made my home
in that.

# For Robert Philen

Somewhere a clock is made of moths,
its hands the color of your leaving.
I write this in the dialect of roots,
the underground language
that trees use to warn each other of drought.

For Robert Philen, who taught me
that the space between words
is where the deer stand at dusk,
breathing fog into the shape of questions.

Consider the river: how it forgets
its own name at every bend,
how it carries the dead leaves
like small, folded letters
never meant to be opened,
only released.

I have been trying to say *love*
in a language older than teeth,
older than the first hunger.
The word keeps dissolving
into weather, into the particular
gray of November skies
that means both *ending*
and *not yet.*

Somewhere you are still walking
through a field that doesn't exist,
and the grass grows upward
into syllables, into the long
vowel sounds of everything
we couldn't finish saying.

Mortality is just a small door
in a house made of seasons.
I keep finding it unlocked,
keep finding your name
written in frost on the windows,
already melting,
already becoming
something else the morning
will have to translate.

For Robert Philen—
this poem is a nest
built from the bones of birds
that haven't died yet,
that are still singing
somewhere in the throat
of the world,
still deciding
what shape
the ending
should take.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse poem with long, flowing sentences using colons and parentheses, exploring themes of naming, memory, and impermanence, dedicated to a specific person.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Water Keeps**
*for my grandmother, Rosalie, who named everything twice*

---

Consider how you gave me my name twice: once
in the hospital light, official, inked onto paper
that has since yellowed in some drawer I'll never open again,
and once in the kitchen, murmured over rising bread
(a name that meant *small bird*, a name that meant *stay*)—
as if one word could be trusted to hold a whole life,
as if naming were not already a kind of forgetting,
the way we call a river by a single word
though it is never the same water twice: the Heraclitus
you never read but somehow always knew, standing
at the stove, stirring something that would not
keep, saying *eat now, eat while it's warm*, because
you understood what I am only learning—
that everything worth naming is already leaving.

I think of you the way I think of snow: briefly,
brilliantly, and always too late to catch it
in the hand before it becomes water, becomes
nothing, becomes the memory of cold
on a palm that has long since forgotten
what it felt like to hold you (your hands,
I mean, which smelled of onion and lavender,
which I did not think to memorize
because I thought—the way children think—
that some things simply do not end).

And now I write your name down here: Rosalie,
which means *rose*, which means (if the old books
are to be believed) *famous*, though you were famous
only to me, only in this small country
of our kitchen, our two chairs by the window,
the plants you named after your sisters
(Bettina, who was always thirsty; Marguerite,
who bloomed too early and then not at all)—
and I wonder if this is what it means to be
remembered: not the fact of you, solid
and singular, but this scatter of almosts,
this handful of syllables I keep turning over
like stones I found once on a beach I can no longer
place on any map, though I know
the tide is still moving there, indifferent,
patient, erasing and rewriting the shore
with each return: the way you did, the way
I try to now, saying your name
into this poem as if it were still summer,
as if you might still answer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental prose-poem in the style of a modernist elegy, mixing floral imagery (lilies, asters, trillium) with reflections on identity and time, addressed to "Robert Philen."
counterfactuals.output:
**For Robert Philen, in the Persistent Tense**

---

Robert Philen, the lilies do not know your name
and this is the first mercy.

They open anyway. White throats, that particular
arrogance of trumpet-flowers who believe
morning is a personal invitation.

*Trillium* — I write it because it sounds
like a small architecture, a three-legged
stool for a three-legged truth: *were, are, will have been.*

You are somewhere in one of these tenses.
I am trying to remember which.

---

The asters come later, always later,
purple hesitations at the field's edge,
as if color itself grew shy toward autumn.

Robert Philen, were you ever this specific —
a name pinned like a specimen
to the corkboard of somebody's afternoon?

I keep saying your name to keep the syntax honest.
Language wants to slide into *he* and *him*,
into the safe pronoun-distance of the dead
or the merely absent, which are not, I'm told,
the same country, though they share a border
guarded by the same white flowers.

---

*Lily* is Latin for something I've forgotten.
*Trillium* for triad, for the leaf that will not
settle into single or into pair.
You, too, refused the simple count —
were you one man or several,
the boy who first said *Robert* to himself
in some kitchen, some Tuesday,
and the man who later couldn't recognize
the word in his own mouth?

---

Time is a bad florist. It arranges us
without asking what we meant to be arrangement of.

Here: lilies for the throat that speaks.
Here: asters for the hour that hesitates.
Here: trillium, unclassifiable, for you,
Robert Philen, who I address
not because you will answer
but because the grammar of elegy
requires a *you*,
requires the pretense of a hearing
into which I can pour
this whole greenhouse of dying light.

---

If identity is only the shape a name makes
in another person's mouth,
then you are still here, slightly,
in the shape of *Robert Philen*
forming and unforming
on this page,
a flower that is also the word for flower,
a man who is also the sound of missing him.

The lilies close at dusk. This is not a metaphor.
This is only what lilies do.

And you, wherever you are keeping time
(if keeping is still the verb, if time
is still the noun) —

Robert Philen —

the trillium keeps blooming in threes
as if three could hold what one could not:
the was, the is, the whatever-comes-after
that we call, for lack of better grammar,
*you.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense, lyrical poem that plays with grammar and syntax—paratactic clauses, parenthetical asides—to express love and existential awareness of death, ending on the idea of home as absence.
counterfactuals.output:
**Provisional**

Say the light does this—falls through the kitchen window slant and yellow, lands on your wrist (the one I've memorized, the blue map under skin), and I think: this, this is the ordinary weight of staying alive together, and it will end.

Not a threat. A fact, folded small enough to carry.

You pour the coffee. I watch your hands and think of hands that stop, of rooms that empty out their voices one by one (my grandmother's room, the smell of it still arriving sometimes, uninvited), and I do not say this, I say pass the sugar, I say did you sleep, because love is also what we don't say into the small clock-ticking rooms we borrow.

We are two accidents who found each other and called it necessary. We are dust that learned to miss things in advance.

Here is what I know: the body is a rented coat. Here is what I don't: how long the lease.

And still—your laugh in the next room, unguarded, a small bell I didn't know I was listening for until it rang and something in my chest unlocked, gently, like a door that was never really stuck, just waiting for the right hand.

I want to tell you every day is a sentence we're writing without punctuation, clause after clause, and and and, no periods yet, please, not yet—

but grammar fails at the edges of this. Language keeps trying to fence the field and the field keeps being larger than the fence.

So: home. Let's talk about home.

Not the house. Not the door with your coat on it, not the bed shaped like two decades of sleep. I mean the thing under the thing—

I mean how home was always this: your voice calling from another room, and me not yet answering, still savoring the seconds before I have to leave this quiet and go be found—

I mean home is the sound of you almost here.
I mean home is what's left when you're not—

the coat on its hook. The coffee going cold. The exact blue of a wrist I no longer get to hold,
and the terrible, tender architecture built entirely
out of your absence,
out of the shape you left in the air
when you were the air
I didn't know I was breathing.

# Instructions for a Portrait Never Finished

I have tried to paint you in snow—
that failed medium, honest for an hour
before it forgets itself, goes clear,
goes ground. You melted through
every version. Still I kept the brush wet.

Call this devotion or call it
the wrong tool for the job. I am asking
whether radio waves remember
the shape of the voice that made them,
once they've traveled so far from the mouth.
I am asking if you do.

You are a woman who eats breakfast,
who forgets umbrellas, who is late
on Tuesdays for reasons
both boring and true—
and also: the tide has your patience,
the moon your particular
way of insisting on return.

Some nights I hear you the way you hear
a song already ending—
that ache of arriving
in the middle of the only verse
that mattered, no way back
to the beginning, no replay
that doesn't already grieve
the first listening.

The flowers on the table are not
a metaphor. They are dying
in real time, the way we all are,
which is the only reason
I bother to name them: peony,
larkspur, the ones whose names
I've forgotten, whose color
I'd know anywhere.

I keep failing to represent you—
not because you're too vast
(though you are)
but because the failing
is the closest I can get
to touching what you're made of:
this ordinary miracle,
this mortal weather
wearing, for now, a name I love,
a face the sea keeps rehearsing
in every wave that almost
reaches shore.
